title: Borrowed Antibodies: Passive Immunization, Humanized Monoclonals and IVIG After Myeloma
summary: Compare built and borrowed immunity, see why animal antisera cause anaphylaxis and serum sickness, follow how monoclonal antibodies were humanized, and recognise the polyclonal IgG of immunoglobulin replacement in a treated myeloma patient.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 47 Hit 16 (treated myeloma with cleared M-spikes looks hypogammaglobulinemic; immunoglobulin infusion supplies polyclonal donor IgG with little IgA or IgM), Hit 17 (passive immunization: immediate, short-lived; heterologous antisera risks) and Hit 18 (humanization by CDR grafting or resurfacing; mammalian CHO/HEK expression). Checked against Casadevall 2002, Tharmalingam 2022, Barahona Afonso 2016, Dhar 2019, Patel 2019, O’Donnell 2025, Ye 2021, Lu 2020, Gordon 2024, Baker 2020, Zhang 2022 and Tan 2021 (full text via Europe PMC) and de Silva 2016 (read via a page-fetch tool because the Europe PMC full text is empty). Context added from the sources: “short-lived” passive protection lasts weeks to months; IVIG contains small, variable amounts of IgA and IgM (so “no IgA or IgM” means little, not none) and its IgG subclass distribution varies by product; humanization reduces but does not abolish immunogenicity. Not taught as source-backed fact (pending): the Arthus reaction as a risk of heterologous antisera, and the immunofixation gel appearance of Hit 16 itself, neither of which was found in the sources read; the gel picture is presented only as the pattern expected from IVIG composition and replacement kinetics. Keller 2000 (Clin Microbiol Rev) and Graham 2015 were read via a page-fetch tool but did not cover these points.

objectives: Contrast active and passive immunity in onset, duration and why passive antibody fades.
Describe the early and late reactions to animal-derived antisera and how antibody engineering reduced immunogenicity.
Interpret polyclonal IgG with little IgA or IgM in a treated myeloma patient receiving immunoglobulin replacement.

scenes.title: Three borrowed antibodies
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three patients. (1) A myeloma patient after treatment: the M-spike has gone, IgG is very low, and monthly intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) has been started; immunofixation now shows diffuse IgG with little IgA or IgM. (2) A snakebite patient treated with horse-derived antivenom develops fever, rash and joint pain 10 days later. (3) A drug label reads “trastuzumab, humanized IgG1”. Question token: “Whose antibody is it?”

cues.text: Invented scenario: a treated myeloma patient on monthly intravenous immunoglobulin shows diffuse IgG on immunofixation, with little IgA or IgM.
A snakebite patient given horse antivenom has fever, rash and sore joints ten days later. And a drug label reads: humanized IgG1.
In each case, whose antibody is it, and what does that mean for the lab and the patient?

scenes.title: Built versus borrowed immunity
scenes.altText: Two columns. Active immunity (vaccine or infection): the patient’s own B cells respond; it takes time and doses, but protection is long-lasting. Passive immunity: preformed antibody is given; protection is immediate but generally short-lived (weeks to months, depending on the source) and dose-related, so it must be redosed. Kinetics card: after infusion, IgG falls fast for the first days as it moves into tissues, then slowly as it is catabolised; median serum half-life of IgG about 23 days (IgM about 5.1, IgA about 5.6); IVIG about 2–3 weeks. Example token: rabies post-exposure prophylaxis gives immune globulin together with vaccine for immediate and lasting protection.

cues.text: Active immunity is built: a vaccine or infection makes the patient’s own B cells respond. It takes time, sometimes several doses, but it lasts.
Passive immunity is borrowed: ready-made antibody is given. Protection starts immediately, but it is short-lived, weeks to months, and depends on the dose.

Why it fades: infused IgG first drops quickly as it spreads into tissues, then declines slowly as it is broken down. Median IgG half-life is about twenty-three days, far longer than IgM or IgA at about five days.
So the two are combined when both speed and duration matter: rabies prophylaxis gives immune globulin together with the vaccine.

props.title: Why it fades
lines: IgG t½ ~23 d · IgM, IgA ~5 d

scenes.title: Foreign antibody and how it was tamed
scenes.altText: Animal antiserum card: horse antisera are seen as foreign protein. Early reactions: anaphylaxis, often within about an hour, even without previous exposure to horse protein. Late reaction: serum sickness 5–14 days later, driven by circulating immune complexes and complement activation; risk rises with the amount of foreign protein. Many modern animal-derived products remove the Fc portion (Fab or F(ab′)2). Engineering ladder card: mouse monoclonal (human anti-mouse antibody, HAMA, response speeds clearance and can cause allergic reactions) → chimeric (mouse variable region, human constant region; e.g. rituximab) → humanized (CDR grafting: only the mouse complementarity-determining regions on a human framework; key framework residues may be back-mutated; e.g. trastuzumab) → resurfacing (replace surface-exposed non-human residues) → fully human (transgenic mice or phage display; e.g. daratumumab). Production token: mammalian cells (mostly CHO; also HEK293) for correct folding and glycosylation.

cues.text: Animal antiserum is foreign protein to a human. Anaphylaxis can occur within about an hour, even in someone never exposed to horse protein before.
Serum sickness comes later, five to fourteen days after the dose, from circulating immune complexes and complement activation. Many modern animal products cut off the Fc portion to reduce reactions.

Monoclonals were tamed step by step. Mouse antibodies trigger a human anti-mouse response. Chimeric ones keep only the mouse variable region. Humanized ones graft just the mouse CDRs, the antigen-binding loops, onto a human framework; resurfacing instead swaps only the exposed mouse residues.
Fully human antibodies come from transgenic mice or phage display. These are made in mammalian cells, mostly Chinese hamster ovary cells, so the antibody folds and is glycosylated correctly.

scenes.title: Reading the borrowed IgG
scenes.altText: Treated myeloma card: myeloma and its treatment are common causes of secondary antibody deficiency, and hypogammaglobulinemia is common (IgG below 500 mg/dL in about 64% of tested patients in one large real-world cohort). Immunoglobulin replacement raises serum IgG and is monitored with serum IgG trough levels (excluding paraprotein). IVIG card: pooled plasma from at least 1000 donors; intact IgG with subclasses as in normal serum (varying by product); only small, variable amounts of IgA and IgM. Expected pattern token: polyclonal IgG with low IgA and IgM = infused donor IgG, not immune recovery (an expectation reasoned from IVIG composition and replacement kinetics; no source read describes the immunofixation picture itself). Hook answers: (1) donor IgG from IVIG; (2) serum sickness from horse protein; (3) mouse CDRs on a human framework.

cues.text: In treated myeloma, the disease and its therapy often leave the patient deficient in antibody. In one large real-world cohort, about two thirds of tested patients had hypogammaglobulinemia.
Intravenous immunoglobulin is pooled from a thousand or more donors. It is intact, polyclonal IgG with subclasses close to normal serum, and only small, variable amounts of IgA and IgM.

Replacement raises serum IgG, and that IgG is donor IgG, tracked by trough levels. IgA and IgM are barely replaced, so they stay low; polyclonal IgG with low IgA and IgM points to the infusion, not to recovery.
Hook answers: the myeloma patient’s IgG is donor IgG; the day ten reaction is serum sickness to horse protein; and humanized means mouse CDRs on a human framework.

props.label: Polyclonal IgG, low IgA/IgM = donor IgG

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Passive immunization gives lasting protection” (✓ immediate but weeks to months; redose or add vaccine); “Polyclonal IgG after IVIG shows immune recovery” (✓ it is donor IgG; look at IgA and IgM and the infusion history); “Humanized antibodies cannot provoke anti-drug antibodies” (✓ humanization reduces immunogenicity but does not remove it; alemtuzumab, the first humanized antibody, is among the most immunogenic).

cues.text: Trap one: passive immunization gives lasting protection. No: it is immediate but lasts weeks to months, so it is redosed or paired with a vaccine.
Trap two: polyclonal IgG after IVIG means the immune system has recovered. No: it is donor IgG; check IgA, IgM and the infusion history.

Trap three: humanized antibodies cannot provoke anti-drug antibodies. No: humanization lowers immunogenicity but does not abolish it. Alemtuzumab, the first humanized antibody, is one of the most immunogenic.

scenes.title: A loan, not a salary
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Passive antibody is a LOAN, not a SALARY: you can spend it today, but it runs out and nobody pays it back. A humanized antibody is a mouse KEY cut onto a human KEYRING: only the teeth (the CDRs) are mouse.” Tokens: loan = passive · salary = active · teeth = CDRs. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: passive antibody is a loan, not a salary. You can spend it today, but it runs out. A humanized antibody is a mouse key cut onto a human keyring: only the teeth, the CDRs, are mouse.

Where it breaks: an IgG loan lasts weeks to months, not days; the body can react against foreign antibody, as in serum sickness; humanized antibodies can still trigger anti-drug antibodies; and IVIG carries small amounts of IgA and IgM.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: IgG loan lasts weeks to months

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Passive = immediate, weeks to months · animal sera: anaphylaxis, serum sickness”, “IVIG = donor polyclonal IgG · humanized = mouse CDRs on human framework”.

cues.text: Borrowed antibody protects at once but fades over weeks, foreign animal antibody can cause anaphylaxis or serum sickness, humanized antibodies keep only the mouse CDRs, and polyclonal IgG after immunoglobulin infusion belongs to the donors, not the patient.

props.label: Passive = immediate, weeks–months · animal sera: anaphylaxis, serum sickness
IVIG = donor polyclonal IgG · humanized = mouse CDRs, human framework

explanation.what: Plain language: sometimes the body is given antibodies instead of making them. They work at once but wear off, antibodies from animals can trigger reactions, drug antibodies are engineered to look human, and donated antibody in a patient’s blood is not the patient’s own. Scientific terms: active and passive immunity, immune globulin, hyperimmune globulin, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), heterologous antiserum, anaphylaxis, serum sickness, immune complexes, Fab and F(ab′)2 fragments, human anti-mouse antibody (HAMA), chimeric, humanized and fully human monoclonal antibodies, complementarity-determining region (CDR) grafting, back-mutation, resurfacing, Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) and HEK293 cells, secondary antibody deficiency, IgG trough level.
explanation.why: Passive antibody is the only way to give immediate immunity, so it is used after exposure and in people who cannot respond to vaccines; its fading and its immunogenicity decide how it is dosed. In the lab, donor IgG can be mistaken for the patient’s own recovered immunity.
explanation.measure: Passive protection: immediate, typically weeks to months, dose-related. Median serum half-life of IgG about 23 days, IgM about 5.1 and IgA about 5.6 days; IVIG about 2–3 weeks. Serum sickness after antivenom: 5–14 days (about 90% of early reactions occur within the first hour). IVIG: pooled from at least 1000 donors (up to 100,000); intact IgG with subclasses as in normal serum, varying by product; IgA from under 5 to over 700 µg/mL depending on product. Hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG under 500 mg/dL) in about 64% of tested myeloma patients in one real-world cohort.
explanation.differs: Active (own B cells, slow, lasting) vs passive (preformed, immediate, fading); animal antiserum (foreign protein, reactions) vs human immune globulin; murine vs chimeric vs humanized vs fully human monoclonal; donor polyclonal IgG vs endogenous immune recovery vs a monoclonal M-protein.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the onset and duration of passive immunization, the reaction days after horse antiserum, what CDR grafting keeps from the mouse, or the meaning of polyclonal IgG with little IgA or IgM in a treated myeloma patient.

Key framework residues may be back-mutated (e.g. trastuzumab)

mnemonic.text: Passive antibody is a LOAN, not a SALARY: you can spend it today, but it runs out. A humanized antibody is a mouse KEY cut onto a human KEYRING: only the teeth (the CDRs) are mouse.
mnemonic.explanation: Separates borrowed from built immunity and pins down which part of a humanized antibody stays non-human.
mnemonic.limitation: An IgG loan lasts weeks to months rather than days; the body can react against foreign antibody (serum sickness, anti-drug antibodies); humanized antibodies can still be immunogenic; IVIG carries small amounts of IgA and IgM.

analogyLimitations: Antibody structures and gel patterns are described schematically, not shown as real images.
Half-lives are median values; the immune status of the patient changes them.
The immunofixation picture in the scenario is the pattern expected from IVIG composition, not a gel appearance described in any source read.
takeaway: Borrowed antibody protects at once but fades over weeks, foreign animal antibody can cause anaphylaxis or serum sickness, humanized antibodies keep only the mouse CDRs, and polyclonal IgG after immunoglobulin infusion belongs to the donors, not the patient.

questions.stem: Compared with vaccination, how does passive immunization with immune globulin differ?

options.text: Protection is immediate but lasts only weeks to months
options.rationale: Correct. Preformed antibody acts at once and fades as it is catabolised, so protection is short-lived and dose-related.
Incorrect. This describes neither; vaccines need time but give long-lasting protection, passive antibody is immediate but fades.

options.text: It requires the recipient’s B cells to respond
options.rationale: Incorrect. Passive antibody works regardless of the recipient’s ability to respond, which is why it is used in immunocompromised patients.

options.text: It cannot be given together with a vaccine
options.rationale: Incorrect. In rabies post-exposure prophylaxis immune globulin is given together with vaccine for immediate and lasting protection.

questions.stem: A humanized monoclonal antibody made by CDR grafting contains which non-human sequences?

options.text: Only the complementarity-determining regions, placed on a human framework
options.rationale: Correct. CDR grafting transplants the non-human CDR loops into a human framework to keep specificity while reducing immunogenicity; a few framework residues may be back-mutated.

options.text: The whole variable region, joined to a human constant region
options.rationale: Incorrect. That describes a chimeric antibody such as rituximab.

options.text: The whole antibody, which is murine
options.rationale: Incorrect. Fully murine antibodies provoke a human anti-mouse antibody response.

options.text: None, because humanized antibodies come only from transgenic mice
options.rationale: Incorrect. Fully human antibodies come from transgenic mice or phage display; humanized antibodies keep the mouse CDRs.

questions.stem: A myeloma patient whose M-spike has cleared after treatment receives monthly intravenous immunoglobulin. Immunofixation shows diffuse polyclonal IgG with very little IgA or IgM. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The IgG is mainly infused donor IgG; the patient remains antibody-deficient
options.rationale: Correct. IVIG is pooled polyclonal IgG with only small amounts of IgA and IgM, and replacement is what raises the serum IgG, so this pattern is expected from the infusion rather than from immune recovery.

options.text: The patient’s B cells have fully recovered
options.rationale: Incorrect. IgA and IgM stay low while IVIG supplies IgG, so the IgG here is borrowed, not the patient’s own.
Incorrect. Relapse would show a monoclonal band, not diffuse polyclonal IgG.

options.text: The pattern proves an IgA-producing clone is hidden in the beta region
options.rationale: Incorrect. Nothing here points to a monoclonal band; the low IgA reflects the patient’s deficiency and the IgG-rich infusion.

references.usedFor: Curriculum source: scope and exam framing. Not used as verification.

references.citation: Casadevall A. Passive antibody administration (immediate immunity) as a specific defense against biological weapons. Emerg Infect Dis. 2002;8(8):833-841. doi:10.3201/eid0808.010516
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Passive antibody is the only intervention giving immediate immunity, lasting weeks and possibly months, regardless of host immune status; vaccines need time but give long-lasting protection; antibody and vaccine combined in rabies post-exposure prophylaxis; animal-derived serum had substantial side effects; licensed monoclonals were mouse-human chimeric and humanized.

references.citation: Tharmalingam T, Han X, Wozniak A, Saward L. Polyclonal hyper immunoglobulin: A proven treatment and prophylaxis platform for passive immunization to address existing and emerging diseases. Hum Vaccin Immunother. 2022;18(2):1886560. doi:10.1080/21645515.2021.1886560
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Passive immunity generally short-lived (weeks to months depending on source) and dose-related; useful in people who respond poorly to vaccines; animal-derived products caused immunogenic reactions and serum sickness, reduced in newer products by enzymatic removal of the Fc portion; rabies immune globulin given with vaccine.

references.citation: Barahona Afonso AF, João CM. The Production Processes and Biological Effects of Intravenous Immunoglobulin. Biomolecules. 2016;6(1):15. doi:10.3390/biom6010015
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. IVIG pooled from at least 1000 (up to 100,000) donors; intact IgG with normal subclass distribution; small variable IgA (<5 to >700 µg/mL) and IgM; IVIG half-life about 2–3 weeks; IgG falls fast for 1–7 days (redistribution) then slowly by catabolism; median half-life IgG 23 d, IgM 5.1 d, IgA 5.6 d; FcRn.

references.citation: de Silva HA, Ryan NM, de Silva HJ. Adverse reactions to snake antivenom, and their prevention and treatment. Br J Clin Pharmacol. 2016;81(3):446-452. doi:10.1111/bcp.12739
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool (Europe PMC full text was empty). Severe anaphylaxis often within about an hour of antivenom, frequently without previous exposure to equine protein; serum sickness 5–14 days after administration, with circulating immune complexes and complement activation; late-reaction risk rises with the amount of heterologous protein (whole IgG, possibly F(ab′)2). The Arthus reaction is not mentioned.

references.citation: Dhar C, Sasmal A, Varki A. From "Serum Sickness" to "Xenosialitis": Past, Present, and Future Significance of the Non-human Sialic Acid Neu5Gc. Front Immunol. 2019;10:807. doi:10.3389/fimmu.2019.00807
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Serum sickness named for reactions to animal serum components in diphtheria antitoxin given to humans.

references.citation: Patel SY, Carbone J, Jolles S. The Expanding Field of Secondary Antibody Deficiency: Causes, Diagnosis, and Management. Front Immunol. 2019;10:33. doi:10.3389/fimmu.2019.00033
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Multiple myeloma and its treatment are common causes of secondary antibody deficiency; immunoglobulin replacement monitored by serum IgG trough levels; guideline thresholds stated as serum IgG excluding paraprotein.

references.citation: O'Donnell E, Gift T, Yousif Z, et al. Real-world effectiveness of immunoglobulin replacement for hypogammaglobulinemia and infections in multiple myeloma. Blood Adv. 2025;9(15):3780-3789. doi:10.1182/bloodadvances.2024015477
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG < 500 mg/dL) in 2075 of 3231 tested myeloma patients (64.2%); myeloma itself and modern therapies (monoclonal antibodies, CAR-T, bispecifics) cause secondary immune deficiency including hypogammaglobulinemia; immunoglobulin replacement raises IgG levels and significantly reduced hypogammaglobulinemia and infections.

references.citation: Ye C, Chen W, Gao Q, et al. Secondary Immunodeficiency and Hypogammaglobulinemia with IgG Levels of <5 g/L in Patients with Multiple Myeloma: A Retrospective Study Between 2012 and 2020 at a University Hospital in China. Med Sci Monit. 2021;27:e930241. doi:10.12659/msm.930241
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Secondary immunodeficiency in myeloma defined as IgG below 5 g/L on at least two occasions; such patients had significantly higher 1-year and 3-year mortality than myeloma patients without it.

references.citation: Lu RM, Hwang YC, Liu IJ, Lee CC, Tsai HZ, Li HJ, Wu HC. Development of therapeutic antibodies for the treatment of diseases. J Biomed Sci. 2020;27(1):1. doi:10.1186/s12929-019-0592-z
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Murine mAbs provoke HAMA (faster clearance, allergic reactions); chimeric = murine variable + human constant (abciximab, rituximab); CDR grafting transplants non-human CDRs into a human framework; back-mutation of crucial framework residues; humanized mAbs improved clinical tolerance; Table 1 formats (trastuzumab humanized IgG1, rituximab chimeric IgG1); daratumumab fully human from transgenic mice; fully human from phage display and transgenic mice; genes expressed in mammalian cell lines.

references.citation: Gordon GL, Raybould MIJ, Wong A, Deane CM. Prospects for the computational humanization of antibodies and nanobodies. Front Immunol. 2024;15:1399438. doi:10.3389/fimmu.2024.1399438
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Experimental humanization approaches: CDR grafting, SDR grafting, framework shuffling and resurfacing (replacing surface-exposed non-human residues while keeping the non-human framework, since buried residues are thought not to affect immunogenicity).

references.citation: Baker D, Ali L, Saxena G, et al. The Irony of Humanization: Alemtuzumab, the First, But One of the Most Immunogenic, Humanized Monoclonal Antibodies. Front Immunol. 2020;11:124. doi:10.3389/fimmu.2020.00124
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Humanization (removing rodent constant regions and grafting CDRs onto human frameworks) reduced immunogenicity, but alemtuzumab, the first humanized antibody, induces anti-drug antibodies rapidly in most people with MS.

references.citation: Zhang JH, Shan LL, Liang F, Du CY, Li JJ. Strategies and Considerations for Improving Recombinant Antibody Production and Quality in Chinese Hamster Ovary Cells. Front Bioeng Biotechnol. 2022;10:856049. doi:10.3389/fbioe.2022.856049
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Recombinant antibodies need post-translational modification (glycosylation), folding and correct cleavage, so mammalian cells are the dominant production system; glycosylation affects activity, immunogenicity and metabolism.

references.citation: Tan E, Chin CSH, Lim ZFS, Ng SK. HEK293 Cell Line as a Platform to Produce Recombinant Proteins and Viral Vectors. Front Bioeng Biotechnol. 2021;9:796991. doi:10.3389/fbioe.2021.796991
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Most therapeutic biopharmaceuticals are produced in CHO cells; mammalian cells allow complex post-translational modifications; human HEK293 cells give more human-like modifications.

claims.text: Passive immunity is immediate, short-lived (weeks to months) and dose-related; active immunity is slower but long-lasting; rabies prophylaxis combines both.
Infused IgG falls by redistribution then catabolism; median half-life IgG 23 d, IgM 5.1 d, IgA 5.6 d; IVIG about 2–3 weeks.
Animal antisera: anaphylaxis often within about an hour even without prior exposure; serum sickness 5–14 days later via immune complexes and complement; Fc removal in modern products.
The Arthus reaction as a risk of heterologous antisera (reviewer Hit 17).
claims.note: Not found in the sources read; not taught.

claims.text: HAMA; chimeric, humanized (CDR grafting, back-mutation), resurfacing and fully human antibodies; examples rituximab, trastuzumab, daratumumab.
Humanization reduces but does not abolish immunogenicity; alemtuzumab is highly immunogenic.
Mammalian cells (mostly CHO, also HEK293) are used for correct folding and glycosylation.
IVIG composition: pooled ≥1000 donors (up to 100,000), intact polyclonal IgG with subclasses as in normal serum but varying by product, small variable IgA and IgM.

Myeloma and its treatment cause secondary antibody deficiency; hypogammaglobulinemia is common (IgG < 500 mg/dL in about 64% of tested patients in one cohort); replacement monitored by IgG troughs excluding paraprotein.

Immunoglobulin replacement raises the patient’s serum IgG, which is why replacement is followed by IgG trough levels; the IgG supplied is pooled donor IgG and IgA and IgM are present only in small amounts.
The immunofixation picture in a treated myeloma patient on immunoglobulin infusion (diffuse polyclonal IgG with little or no IgA or IgM), as described in reviewer Hit 16.

The lesson presents it only as the pattern expected from IVIG composition and replacement kinetics (claims cl-ivig and cl-igrt-igg), not as a documented description; searches of Europe PMC for immunofixation after immunoglobulin replacement found nothing.

“A loan, not a salary; mouse key on a human keyring.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 47 Hit 17 calls passive immunization short-lived and lists anaphylaxis, serum sickness and Arthus reactions for heterologous antisera. Casadevall 2002 and Tharmalingam 2022 give the duration as weeks to months (dose- and source-dependent), and Tharmalingam 2022 notes that many modern animal-derived products remove the Fc portion to reduce reactions; the Arthus reaction was not found in the sources read and is not taught (register flag rv-passive-immunization-context).

Ch. 47 Hit 16 says immunofixation shows polyclonal IgG from immunoglobulin infusions with NO IgA or IgM. Barahona Afonso 2016 reports that IVIG contains small, variable amounts of IgA (from under 5 to over 700 µg/mL by product) and IgM, so the lesson teaches little IgA or IgM rather than none. No source read describes the immunofixation appearance itself, so that gel picture is held as a pending claim (cl-ife-pattern) and taught only as the pattern expected from IVIG composition; the hypogammaglobulinemia half of Hit 16 is taught directly from Patel 2019, O’Donnell 2025 and Ye 2021 (register flag rv-ivig-ife-iga-traces).

Ch. 47 Hit 18 says humanization cuts immunogenicity while keeping specificity. Baker 2020 shows humanization reduces but does not abolish immunogenicity (alemtuzumab, the first humanized antibody, induces anti-drug antibodies in most treated MS patients), and Lu 2020 notes framework back-mutations are often needed to keep binding; Tan 2021 describes CHO as the main production line with HEK293 used for human-like modifications (register flag rv-humanization-residual-immunogenicity).

morphology.note: No gel images or structural renderings; antibodies and patterns shown as schematic cards.
